blocks.text: **The task.** There are piles of bananas and `h` hours available. At a chosen speed of K bananas per hour, each hour is spent on a single pile — finishing it, or eating K from it. Find the smallest K that clears every pile within `h` hours.
Another "minimum X such that it fits" problem, so the structure is identical — only the bounds and the check change.

items: **Upper bound:** `max(piles)`. At that speed every pile takes exactly one hour, which is the fastest the rules allow.

blocks.text: Why the ceiling is the whole problem
`Math.ceil(pile / speed)` encodes the rule that an hour cannot be shared between piles.

A pile of 7 at speed 3 takes ⌈7/3⌉ = 3 hours: two full hours and one hour eating just 1 banana. That leftover hour is wasted, and plain division would hide it. Miss the ceiling and the check silently reports fewer hours than reality.
Why the upper bound is not the sum

For the shipping problem the ceiling was the sum of all weights. Here it is the maximum pile, because speed beyond that changes nothing — you still spend one full hour per pile. Going higher only adds useless iterations.
Choosing tight, justified bounds is the part of this pattern that requires actual thought; the loop is boilerplate.
**Time: O(N log M)** where M is the largest pile. **Space: O(1)**.
